{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-nj-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"085fd6ddd6116599407c9b8af74f5f12f24d7be6a1f472155c6f078f82355c32","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nj-class-d:lineage:24","source_registry_sha256":"057b72c7c679c997f56ae00ef97a6b14dbe264551f4121b9bf67b0457d9cf7c1","source_liveness_sha256":"1ca7bfbb9e3c0a6b19e5e808ecab6fe8329f3b4799e394abc260d65c1d6513e7"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C2"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C2","chunk_id":"C2.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Rules-of-the-road confusables and highway details","heading":"C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: speed limit tiers, center line markings, yielding rules, highway lanes and left-turn positions","learner_facing":false,"markdown":"## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: speed limit tiers, center line markings, yielding rules, highway lanes and left-turn positions
Confusable pairs among speed, passing, yielding and highway rules, followed by continuation facts the C block left out for size; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec06-R01 | anchor: A01
The two lowest default limits are easy to swap: 25 mph covers school zones and business or residential districts, while 35 mph covers suburban business and residential districts. [A01]
Why it matters: group speed limits; confusable urban versus suburban limit.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec06-R02 | anchor: A01
The two highway limits are also easy to swap: 55 mph applies to certain posted state highways and to interstates, while 65 mph applies only to certain posted interstate highways. [A01]
Why it matters: group speed limits; confusable fifty-five versus sixty-five.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec06-R03 | anchor: A03
Center line markings read from your own side: two solid lines forbid passing, a broken line on your side permits it, and two broken lines permit it from both sides. [A03]
Why it matters: group passing; confusable solid versus broken lines.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec06-R04 | anchor: A06
A multi-way stop gives the right-of-way to the driver on the right when two arrive together, while a yield sign requires slowing and giving way to the crossing road's traffic. [A06]
Why it matters: group intersections; confusable stop versus yield control.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec06-R05 | anchor: A07
When it is unclear who has the right-of-way in a traffic circle, fall back on the basic uncontrolled-intersection rule: the vehicle on the left yields to the vehicle approaching from the right. [A07]
Why it matters: group intersections; confusable circle versus crossroad.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec06-R06 | anchor: A08
An acceleration lane is for speeding up and should not be stopped in, while a deceleration lane is where you start slowing down and obey its advisory speed. [A08]
Why it matters: group highways; confusable acceleration versus deceleration lane.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec06-R07 | anchor: A02
Even a small increase in speed sharply raises the risk that a pedestrian struck in a crash is badly hurt or killed, and lower speeds greatly improve pedestrian survival. [A02]
Why it matters: group speed; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec06-R08 | anchor: A02
Some crashes are caused by driving too slowly or backing up in traffic; if a vehicle problem keeps you from keeping up, pull safely off the road and turn on the hazard lights. [A02]
Why it matters: group speed; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec06-R09 | anchor: A03
Highways are designated Safe Corridors when their crash rate is 50 percent above the state rate and at least 1,000 crashes were reported over three years. [A03]
Why it matters: group passing and fines; difficulty high.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec06-R10 | anchor: A04
Buses and postal vehicles re-entering the flow of traffic are given the right-of-way. [A04]
Why it matters: group yielding; difficulty low.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec06-R11 | anchor: A05
Yield to people using motorized or mobility-assistance devices in a crosswalk or trying to cross, and to other vehicles already inside the intersection. [A05]
Why it matters: group yielding; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec06-R12 | anchor: A05
Crosswalks may be marked or unmarked, and one exists at every corner of an intersection unless signs prohibit pedestrians from crossing there. [A05]
Why it matters: group pedestrians; misconception only painted crosswalks count.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec06-R13 | anchor: A06
Watch carefully for pedestrians when turning, including right turns on red, and before any turn scan left, right and behind and check mirrors and blind spots for cyclists and pedestrians. [A06]
Why it matters: group pedestrians; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec06-R14 | anchor: A06
Cutting through private property to get around a traffic signal or sign is a motor vehicle violation. [A06]
Why it matters: group intersections; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec06-R15 | anchor: A07
On rural roads trees or crops, and elsewhere buildings, parked cars or bushes, can block the view of cross traffic, so slow down or stop fully before going ahead. [A07]
Why it matters: group intersections; difficulty low.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec06-R16 | anchor: A08
Most exit ramps and deceleration lanes are on the right; when an exit is on the left, follow the signs that direct traffic to the proper exit lane. [A08]
Why it matters: group highways; difficulty medium.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec06-R17 | anchor: A10
On highways through cities, drive in the left or center lane during rush hour to avoid merge conflicts, and look for your exit early. [A10]
Why it matters: group highways; difficulty medium.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec06-R18 | anchor: A10
When you see a disabled vehicle ahead, slow down and leave more space, possibly by changing lanes, and watch for pedestrians, tow trucks and police. [A10]
Why it matters: group highways; difficulty low.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec06-R19 | anchor: A10
At toll plazas, slow down early because traffic may back up, look for green lights marking open booths, and check both sides for merging traffic when leaving. [A10]
Why it matters: group highways; difficulty low.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec06-R20 | anchor: A11
Enter a curve by slowing down beforehand and staying out of other lanes, and watch for vehicles drifting into yours. [A11]
Why it matters: group curves; difficulty low.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec06-R21 | anchor: A11
Bicycles, mopeds and other hard-to-see vehicles may have a green light while you turn right on red, so look for them before turning. [A11]
Why it matters: group turning; misconception red-light turn has a clear road.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec06-R22 | anchor: A11
At a cloverleaf interchange, watch for the entrance and exit signs and drive slowly through the loop at the posted speed. [A11]
Why it matters: group highways; difficulty low.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec06-R23 | anchor: A12
For a left turn from a two-way road onto another two-way road, approach close to the line nearest the center of the road and keep to the right of the center line of the road you enter. [A12]
Why it matters: group turning; confusable two-way versus four-lane left turn.
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec06-R24 | anchor: A12
Solid lines between intersections mark no-passing zones, but they may be crossed carefully when turning into or out of a driveway in a business or residential area. [A12]
Why it matters: group turning; misconception solid lines can never be crossed.
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0075]
